content: The ABO histo-blood group system transferase is an enzyme with glycosyltransferase activity, encoded by the ABO gene in humans. This enzyme is expressed in a wide range of tissues and cell types. The ABO gene determines an individual's blood group by modifying the oligosaccharides present on cell surface glycoproteins. Variations in the protein sequence among individuals dictate the type of modification and, consequently, the blood group. The ABO gene contains one of 27 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with an increased risk of coronary artery disease. It is composed of seven exons and encodes three alleles. The A allele produces α-1,3-N-acetylgalactosamine transferase (A-transferase), which facilitates the transfer of GalNAc residues from the UDP-GalNAc donor nucleotide to the Gal residues of the H antigen, converting the H antigen into the A antigen in individuals with A and AB blood types. The B allele encodes α-1,3-galactosyltransferase (B-transferase), which transfers Gal residues from the UDP-Gal donor nucleotide to the Gal residues of the H antigen, converting the H antigen into the B antigen in individuals with B and AB blood types. Interestingly, the difference between the A and B glycosyltransferase enzymes is only four amino acids. In contrast, the O allele results in a frameshift mutation, leading to the production of a protein that cannot modify oligosaccharides ending in fucose linked to galactose. As a result, individuals with the O blood group lack A or B antigens, and the unmodified sugar structure is referred to as the H antigen. These antigens are critical for compatibility in blood transfusions and organ transplantation. Additionally, other minor alleles of the ABO gene have been identified. In individuals of European descent, six common alleles of the ABO gene are observed. Nearly all humans exhibit a phenotype that is a combination of these six alleles: A101 (A1), A201 (A2), B101 (B1), O01 (O1), O02 (O1v), and O03 (O2). Numerous rare variants of these alleles have also been identified in human populations worldwide. The ABO alleles and their encoded glycosyltransferases have been implicated in various oncologic conditions. Studies using anti-GTA/GTB monoclonal antibodies have shown that the loss of these enzymes correlates with malignant transformations in bladder and oral epithelial tissues. Furthermore, the expression of ABO blood group antigens in normal human tissues depends on the differentiation state of the epithelium. In most human carcinomas, including oral carcinoma, a significant reduction in the expression of A and B antigens is a key event in tumor development. Several studies have reported a relative downregulation of GTA and GTB in oral carcinomas, which is associated with tumor progression. More recently, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified variants in the ABO locus that are linked to susceptibility to pancreatic cancer. Additionally, a multi-locus genetic risk score study, incorporating 27 loci including the ABO gene, has identified individuals at increased risk for both incident and recurrent coronary artery disease events. This study also demonstrated an enhanced clinical benefit from statin therapy in these individuals. The findings were based on data from the Malmö Diet and Cancer study, as well as four randomized controlled trials: JUPITER, ASCOT (primary prevention cohorts), and CARE, PROVE IT-TIMI 22 (secondary prevention cohorts).
